title: Futures Slide As AI Unwind Goes Global: Kospi Crashes Into Bear Market, Treasuries Soar
desc:
Futures Slide As AI Unwind Goes Global: Kospi Crashes Into Bear Market, Treasuries Soar

US futures are lower as the AI unwind goes global - Korea's Kospi crashed into a bear market and tripped circuit breakers, CoreWeave bonds sank deeper into distress and Anthropic's still-blistering but slowing growth failed to impress - while yesterday's hot CPI scare has morphed into a growth scare; as a result Treasuries are ripping higher with 10Y yields tumbling 10bps to 5.08%, the lowest since Sept. 23. As of 6:20am ET, S&P futures are 0.3% lower at 7,749 while Nasdaq futures slide 1.1% to 29,857 and Dow futures are up 0.2%; small caps are the odd man out with Russell 2000 futures up 0.3%. Yesterday the S&P 500 fell 1.1% to its worst day since July, the Nasdaq 100 lost 2% and the SOX dropped for a sixth straight session. Premarket, Mag-7 and AI baskets are all lower with Apple the only Mag 7 name in the green; chipmakers, memory, neoclouds and AI infrastructure names are all sliding, with CoreWeave down another 6-7% after imploding 15% yesterday as its bonds traded at distressed levels. The day's driver is AI financing (again): Anthropic's $16.8 billion Q3 revenue implies slowing growth, and a Gartner report that $3,5 trillion of AI infrtastructure spending could be exposed to impairment by 2030 is making the rounds. Bonds rally across the curve in a bull flattener with yields down 7-11bps, as the AI selloff pushes investors into havens and odds of an October Fed hike slide back to around 30% from a post-CPI intraday peak of 58%; bunds and gilts also rally about 10bps, helped by the pullback in energy. The dollar is lower, with the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index down 0.3%-0.4% and the Swiss franc leading G-10 gains while the Aussie slumps after a weak jobs report. In commodities, Brent drops almost 2% to $104 on the risk-off tone and talk of the US easing shadow fleet sanctions, gold jumps 1.3% to $4,158 and silver is up 2.1%, while copper slides. Bitcoin is down 0.6% near $81,200. US economic data slate includes September retail sales, PPI, October Empire manufacturing and Philly Fed, and weekly jobless claims (all 8:30am) and August business inventories (10am). Fed speaker slate includes Goolsbee (10am), Hammack (4:30pm) and Chair Warsh, who has a fireside chat with the IMF's Georgieva in Bangkok at 11:30pm ET before the blackout. Treasury sells $110 billion of 4-week and $105 billion of 8-week bills at 11:30am.

In premarket trading, Apple (AAPL) outperforms the group during the AI selloff (AAPL +0.8%, Microsoft -0.5%, Alphabet -0.8%, Meta Platforms -1%, Tesla -1.4%, Amazon -1.8%, Nvidia -1.6%)

  • Chipmakers and other AI-related firms slide after Anthropic disclosed third-quarter revenue that likely slowed from the previous quarter. Among notable movers: CoreWeave (CRWV) -3%, Dell (DELL) -4%, Micron (MU) -4%, Intel (INTC) -3%, Marvell (MRVL) -4%, AMD (AMD) -3%, Broadcom (AVGO) -2%
  • AngloGold Ashanti (AU) rises 3% after Goldman Sachs initiated coverage at buy, citing increased central-bank purchases that should support gold prices. Gold is also higher on Thursday morning.
  • Cirrus Logic (CRUS) slips 2% after being downgraded to sector weight at KeyBanc, which sees a weak outlook for the Apple supplier.
  • FMC Corp. (FMC) sinks 27% after the agricultural chemicals firm cut its third quarter outlook.
  • Fortrea Holdings (FTRE) gains 3% after Deutsche Bank upgraded the health services firm to buy, citing potential for revenue growth and margin expansion.
  • Kimberly-Clark (KMB) climbs 3% after the household products company reported preliminary net sales for the third quarter that met the average analyst estimate.
  • Penske Automotive Group (PAG) climbs 8% after entering a deal to be taken private for $212 per share in cash by Penske Corp. and Mitsui.
  • Quantinuum (QNT) rises 3% as Morgan Stanley upgrades to overweight, saying the stock offers the most attractive valuation among peers.
  • Rocket Lab (RKLB) falls 11% after adjusting the target launch timing for its Neutron medium-lift rocket, with the vehicle’s inaugural launch now expected to occur in 2027.
  • Walmart (WMT) gains 2.8% after Deutsche Bank upgraded the retailer to buy, citing a favorable setup into 2027.

In other corporate news, the US FTC has subpoenaed Anthropic and OpenAI seeking documentation in relation to safety incidents and privacy policies, Axios reports, just as the AI sector needed one more thing to worry about. IDC said the smartphone market suffered its worst decline on record in the September quarter, with rising memory costs pushing shipments down 22% and "the worst is yet to come." Rocket Lab drops almost 10% after delaying the inaugural Neutron launch to 2027, while IonQ filed to offer about $2 billion in shares and warrants. Barclays analysts said a Tesla-SpaceX merger has become widely expected and an announcement could come before Tesla's annual general meeting. Marsh will shoulder a larger share of the CS-Greensill settlement, the FT reports; EasyJet shareholders are being asked to support an Apollo takeover proposal; VW is pivoting to trucks and rugged SUVs in a quest for US profit; and Iambic Therapeutics raised $150 million in a US IPO priced at the midpoint. Schwab, Marsh McLennan, US Bancorp, PNC, BNY and Prologis report before the open, with Interactive Brokers, Alcoa and JB Hunt after the close.

The global AI unwind is gaining momentum: negative headlines are piling up, from signs of Anthropic's slowing growth to CoreWeave bonds plunging into distress and Gartner's warning that $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030. Even good results from TSMC - a Q4 revenue guide of $52.3-54.3 billion against a street at about $50 billion - failed to dispel the concerns, and a global selloff in semis dragged South Korea's benchmark down nearly 8% into a bear market, while the SOX is down 12% over the past six sessions, as Goldman warned of a semi "air pocket" last week.

As discussed last night, Anthropic's pre-IPO investor event failed to impress as the revenue growth shared was well below the double digit growth observed earlier in the year. “In any normal world, companies would kill for 45% q/q growth,” said Vital Knowledge founder Adam Crisafulli. “But in the land of AI, where investors are used to parabolic figures, a slowdown in growth undercuts sentiment.”

The market is especially worried about the financing model of neocloud companies, which are borrowing huge amounts at high rates to build data centers. CoreWeave's 5Y CDS closed at 1,118bps yesterday, up a massive 136bps, and its debt due 2032 dropped below 78 cents on the dollar - paper investors bought at par just four months ago! CoreWeave, for its part, said it isn't worried about the market's reaction and wants access to "unlimited" pools of money (what could go wrong). Meanwhile, hyperscaler capex is expected to total more than $3 trillion over the next three years, which is a lot of money to finance with 10Y yields north of 5%.

“AI stocks in EM will be the first to go, given their outperformance this year,” said Vey-Sern Ling, a managing director at Union Bancaire Privee. “Higher rates and USD also hurt EM tech disproportionately.”

“The market is juggling a number of risks at the moment, notably geopolitical, which is fueling oil prices and in turn inflation and monetary policy,” said Roland Kaloyan at Societe Generale. Some investors “are looking to take profits and rotate out of the semiconductor trade. With yields where they are today, bonds are becoming increasingly attractive.”

That said, yesterday's hot CPI hasn't gone away: headline CPI rose 0.65% m/m and core 0.335% vs 0.2% expected, briefly lifting October hike odds above 50% before the AI rout unwound the entire move. Deutsche Bank's Henry Allen thinks the market is too complacent.

“The 50 risk is live,” Henry Allen, macro strategist at Deutsche Bank Research, said in an interview with Bloomberg TV, warning that the more the Fed stays behind the curve, “the risk is they have to play catch up.” Markets are grappling with offsetting forces, “where AI is pushing down the one side, CPI is pushing up on the other, but the risks are definitely on the hawkish side.”

JPM's Market Intel desk under Andrew Tyler stays Tactically Bullish, noting the two big questions yesterday were the reversal in bond yields and how much longer the tech selloff can run. On the former, the team blames a market that clearly overreacted when October hike odds jumped above 50%, a move into quality and safe assets, and "concern about a possible AI-related credit event." On tech, the SOXX fell for a seventh straight day; with JPM's TPM positioning at a neutral ~46th percentile vs ~19th near the late-July lows, the desk sees potential for further de-grossing into key tech catalysts, but says "we remain constructive on the sector and still see a possible opportunity to buy the dip." JPM FX sales' Steve Bruner put it more colorfully: "Have rates finally crossed the AI Rubicon? My instinct is Not Yet."

Goldman's desks spent the night counting casualties. In London, Rich Privorotsky writes that the GS global neocloud basket is down 20% in five sessions, "a roughly 1st pctl move over ten years", adding that "in hindsight, the pain trade was long AI/ short bonds. Now we're watching both sides unwind." His conclusion: "the market is discovering that demand for compute can grow exponentially, but the capital available to finance it cannot." Praneet Shah echoes that "the cost of financing the AI buildout is starting to collide with how much the market can comfortably absorb", while Gen Sales' Dioni Ellinikaki notes that in an increasingly debt-funded capex cycle, "access to credit is becoming the key constraint rather than AI adoption itself." On the damage: GS Prime shows TMT-focused funds lost 2.7% on the day (a -2.6 standard deviation move), and the TMT desk's info-tech sell skew was the highest in more than four weeks. In Asia, Rachel Hu notes the TAIEX saw a record ~$9.3 billion foreign outflow, yet market color "suggested limited capitulation versus the July selloff" — a polite way of saying there may be more to come.

In Europe, French bonds remain in focus: the OAT-bund spread widened 1bp to 142bps, just shy of Monday's closing peak, as France sold €12 billion of bonds at the top of its target range. Former ECB chief Mario Draghi said the ECB is unlikely to step in any time soon with market intervention to help France, setting a high bar for the TPI.

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is down 0.1% at 637.05, with 225 members down and 369 up, as investors turn to defensive sectors while the global tech selloff gathers pace; telecoms, food & beverage and insurance lead, while tech, basic resources and industrials lag. The FTSE 100 is up 0.5% thanks to its low tech exposure, while the Euro Stoxx 50 drops 0.6% and the DAX is down 0.3%. ASML falls 5.5%, ASM International 9.1% and BE Semi 6.1%; JPM notes Semis, AI Data Centers and Momentum Longs baskets are showing 1-3z moves, while AI Disruptions and Luxury outperform. Here are the biggest European movers:

  • Ericsson shares surge as much as 11% after the 5G gear maker reported sales and profits ahead of expectations, driven by its core networks business and projects in Japan and India.
  • Pernod Ricard shares gain as much as 4% after analysts broadly welcomed the beverage maker’s first-quarter results, noting improved momentum in the US and China and signs the quarter marked a low-point for the company.
  • THG surges as much as 17% after the nutrition and beauty company upgraded its profit guidance, which Peel Hunt says is likely to trigger increases to consensus estimates.
  • EQT rises as much as 4.7% after the alternative investment firm reported an increase in assets under management driven by Coller Capital, which the firm acquired earlier this year.
  • Dunelm gains as much as 7.6% after analysts said the UK home-furnishings retailer’s first-quarter trading update was better than analysts had expected, driven by a recent sales improvement.
  • TotalEnergies shares rise as much as 1.1% after the French energy company published its 3Q trading statement. Analysts tout strong refining margins while oil and gas production and LNG also performed above expectations.
  • DocMorris shares rise as much as 9.4% after the online pharmacy delivered “long-awaited” positive adjusted Ebitda in the third quarter and raised its guidance for the full year.
  • European semiconductor stocks sink on Thursday as Anthropic’s sales growth failed to impress investors that have grown more anxious about the sustainability of AI spending.
  • Entain slides as much as 3.8% after posting softer online net gaming revenue growth due to unfavorable sports results in Italy and a provisional ban on online gambling in Brazil.
  • Workspace shares fall as much as 9.8% after the UK flexible-office landlord said its target of an additional £100m+ of disposals is unlikely to be fully achieved by March 2027.
  • Alfa Laval drops as much as 4.2% as Nordea downgrades its rating on the Swedish industrial equipment maker to hold from buy on a more balanced risk-reward following recent strength in the shares.
  • Kinnevik slides as much as 11% as DNB Carnegie says the Swedish investment company’s third-quarter unlisted net asset value came in “clearly below” expectations.
  • Mining stocks fall across Europe, driven by industrial metals amid a global selloff in the artificial-intelligence trade.

Asian stocks slumped as the semiconductor selloff deepened on concerns over AI financing, with the MSCI Asia Pacific Index falling as much as 3.3%, the most since July 28, and its tech subgauge sinking as much as 7.1%; Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and TSMC were the biggest drags. South Korea's Kospi plunged 7.6%, triggering Level 1 circuit breakers for the first time since July 29 and entering a bear market, as Samsung fell 9.5% and SK Hynix 11.1%, with foreigners net sellers for an 8th straight session. Japan's Nikkei sank 4.9%, its worst day since March, while Taiwan's Taiex fell 3.4% on a record ~$9.3 billion of foreign selling. China's CSI 300 dropped 2% and the Hang Seng lost 1%, while Australia's ASX 200 held up relatively well as financials and defensives offset weakness in tech and miners. India's Nifty bucked the trend, rising 1.9% on rotation and lower crude. Asian central banks stepped in to support their currencies, with Taiwan's state banks selling dollars and the RBI and Bank Indonesia intervening.

In FX, the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is down 0.3%-0.4%, giving back the post-CPI spike as US yields fall; the DXY trades in a 101.87-102.39 range after hitting its highest level since May 2025 on Wednesday. The Swiss franc leads G-10 gains, with USD/CHF down 0.6% to 0.8297, while EUR/USD rises 0.5% to 1.1212 and cable is up 0.4% at 1.325, shrugging off a better-than-expected UK August GDP print. The Aussie is the laggard, down 0.6% to 0.6930 after an unexpected contraction in September employment pushed the jobless rate up to 4.7%, prompting traders to scale back RBA hike bets. USD/JPY edges up 0.2% to 158.0.

In rates, Treasuries extend their advance across the curve in a bull flattener as investors seek havens amid the slump in technology stocks, with the 10-year yield down 10bps to 5.08%, the lowest since Sept. 23 - and a far cry from the 5.33% hit right after yesterday's CPI print. The 2-year yield is down about 8bps at 4.72% after having spiked as much as 16-20bps intraday on Wednesday, while the 30-year falls 7bps to 5.45%. If the rally continues, the Sept. 23 session was the last time a sub-5% 10Y was seen (and for the record, we are still some way off the 5.365% early-October peak). Bunds rally, led by the belly, with the German 10Y falling 10bps to 3.37%, the lowest since Sept. 8, as money markets pare ECB hike bets and no longer fully price three increases by end-2027; gilts jump with the UK 10Y down 9bps to 5.33%, ignoring the GDP beat. Spain sold €5.4 billion and France €12 billion of bonds. In the US, Treasury sells $110 billion of 4-week and $105 billion of 8-week bills at 11:30am, with the focus on PPI and retail sales and then Chair Warsh's final word before the blackout.

SMBC Nikko's Makoto Noji thinks the 10-year yield may be topping out: Wednesday's move was a rare return to the "textbook" pattern - stocks fell and the 10-year yield declined as the curve twist-flattened - which may signal long-term yields are close to peaking, as lower stock prices could prompt higher-income households to rein in spending. Not everyone is convinced; Bloomberg's Vassilis Karamanis argues the move is less a haven trade than a rates trade, with Treasuries rallying "because the tightening already embedded in yields starts doing some of the Fed's work."

In commodities, WTI November is down 0.2% at $94.92 (in a $93.58-95.31 range) and Brent December slides 1.9% to $104.06 (in a $103.64-105.83 range), as the equity selloff pushes investors away from risky bets and the Trump administration considers easing sanctions on shadow fleet vessels to bring down record-high freight rates. That is overshadowing escalation risk: CNN reports the US military has drawn up new strike plans that include potentially using the "mother of all bombs" against Iranian energy and nuclear sites, Ukraine's Zelenskyy has ordered strikes on Russian refineries to resume and a drone strike set the Ryazan refinery on fire overnight, while a cargo ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz after a strike. API data showed an 11.1 million barrel crude draw (vs. a 1.9 million build expected); the delayed EIA report is out at noon and WTI November options expire today. Dutch TTF slips toward €85/MWh. Spot gold rises 1.3% to $4,158 on haven demand and the softer dollar, silver gains 2.1% to $56.72, while LME copper trades near the bottom of a $14,320-14,480/t range.

US economic data slate includes September retail sales, PPI final demand, October Empire manufacturing and Philadelphia Fed business outlook, and initial jobless claims (all 8:30am), August business inventories (10am) and the September federal budget balance (2pm). Fed speaker slate includes Goolsbee (10am) and Hammack (4:30pm), with Chair Warsh in a fireside chat with the IMF's Georgieva at 11:30pm ET.

The IMF-World Bank meetings continue in Bangkok, EU leaders meet for a summit in Brussels, and SEMICON West wraps up in San Francisco.

title: Why Diesel Prices Are So Much Higher Than Gasoline
desc:
Why Diesel Prices Are So Much Higher Than Gasoline

Authored by Robert Rapier via OilPrice.com,

  • Diesel has generally cost more than gasoline since 2004 due to higher production costs, taxes, and global demand.

  • Global refinery disruptions, export restrictions, and low inventories have widened the diesel price premium in 2026.

  • Strong US crude production and refinery output cannot fully offset global diesel supply shortages.

There was a time when diesel fuel was usually cheaper than gasoline in the United States. That relationship began to change about 20 years ago, and since then diesel has generally traded at a premium. Today, that premium is not just persistent but unusually large, which raises an obvious question: how did we get from gasoline typically costing more than diesel to diesel costing substantially more than gasoline?

The answer has two parts.

The first is structural and goes back to the mid-2000s, when changes in fuel specifications, taxes, refining economics, and global demand fundamentally altered the relationship between gasoline and diesel prices.

The second is more immediate. In 2026, refinery disruptions, geopolitical conflicts, low inventories, and reduced exports from major suppliers have pushed the global diesel market into an unusually tight position. Understanding the difference between those long-term and short-term forces explains both why diesel usually costs more and why the gap is so large right now.

Diesel Was Once The Cheaper Fuel

Before the mid-2000s, diesel was often cheaper than regular gasoline in the United States. There were exceptions, particularly during cold winters when heating-oil demand strengthened, but the longer-term pattern generally favored diesel. That began to change around 2004, and according to the Energy Information Administration, on-highway diesel prices have been higher than regular gasoline prices almost continuously since September of that year.

That shift is clearly visible in the historical data I examined in my 2023 article on the subject. In the decade before 2005, gasoline generally traded at a small premium to diesel. After that, the relationship reversed, and diesel became the more expensive fuel in most years. The timing is important because it coincided with a major change in the way U.S. refiners had to produce highway diesel.

Ultra-Low-Sulfur Diesel Changed The Economics

Beginning in the mid-2000s, U.S. refiners had to dramatically reduce the sulfur content of highway diesel. That was an important environmental improvement because sulfur emissions contribute to air pollution and acid rain, but it also made diesel more expensive to produce. Refineries invested billions of dollars in new hydrotreating and sulfur-removal equipment, and those investments increased capital and operating costs and made compliant diesel more expensive to produce and distribute.

My earlier article focused heavily on this transition because the timing lines up closely with the point at which diesel's historical discount disappeared. EIA now describes the persistent diesel premium as the result of several factors working together, including strong global demand for diesel and other distillates, the higher cost of producing low-sulfur diesel, and federal taxes that are six cents per gallon higher on diesel than on gasoline.

None of those factors explains every short-term price movement, but together they created a structural premium that had not existed to the same degree before 2004. Once diesel became more expensive to produce and more tightly linked to global distillate markets, the old relationship with gasoline never really returned.

Diesel Became A Global Commodity

Another important change has been the globalization of the diesel market. Gasoline is also traded internationally, but diesel and other middle distillates occupy an especially important role in the global economy because they power trucking, agriculture, construction, mining, shipping, industrial equipment, and heating systems. Strong demand in Europe, China, India, and the United States has kept pressure on global distillate balances for years.

That means U.S. diesel prices are increasingly influenced by events far beyond U.S. borders. Even when domestic production is strong, refiners can export diesel into higher-priced international markets, tying domestic prices more closely to global supply and demand. This is one reason it is misleading to look only at U.S. crude oil production and assume that abundant domestic oil should automatically translate into cheap diesel.

The United States can produce plenty of crude while still facing tight supplies of refined products. Crude oil has to be processed in the right refineries, into the right products, and then moved through the right transportation system. Those constraints matter just as much as the amount of oil coming out of the ground.

2022 Showed How Quickly The Premium Can Explode

The most dramatic recent example came in 2022, when Russia's invasion of Ukraine disrupted global energy markets. Diesel was hit particularly hard. Russia was a major supplier of crude oil, refined products, and feedstocks to Europe and other markets, so sanctions and trade restrictions forced a rapid reshuffling of global flows. Gasoline prices rose sharply as well, but diesel supplies tightened even more, pushing the diesel premium to record levels.

In my earlier article, I noted that the gasoline-diesel spread reached a record in 2022. At the time, the disruption from Russia explained why a structural premium suddenly became an extreme one. The market eventually adjusted as trade routes shifted, refinery operations stabilized, and inventories recovered, but that normalization did not last.

Why The Gap Is So Large Again In 2026

The current situation resembles 2022 in one important respect: global diesel supply has again been disrupted more severely than gasoline supply. EIA recently reported that global distillate supplies are tight because of reduced refining activity in Russia, China, and the Middle East. At the same time, U.S. refiners have been running near maximum utilization, with domestic distillate production averaging about 5.1 million barrels per day through August, the highest level since 2019.

That point is worth emphasizing because it shows that the current problem is not simply a collapse in U.S. refinery output. American refiners are producing large volumes of diesel, but global demand for those barrels has increased at the same time that supplies elsewhere have fallen. As exports increased, U.S. inventories declined, and by mid-September distillate inventories were about 13% below the five-year seasonal average even though summer is normally a period when inventories build ahead of winter.

Since then, the global situation has become even tighter. Russia has restricted diesel exports as refinery infrastructure has been damaged, China has curtailed fuel exports to protect domestic supplies, and Middle Eastern refining and shipping have been disrupted by the conflict involving Iran. Tanker costs and insurance rates have also risen, making it more expensive to move refined products around the world.

The result is a global scramble for middle distillates. Both gasoline and diesel are affected by higher crude prices, but diesel is being squeezed more severely because the product itself is in shorter supply relative to demand. That is why the diesel-gasoline spread has widened so dramatically.

The Price Gap Is Now Extraordinary

As of October 5, the national average price of on-highway diesel was $6.199 per gallon, compared with $4.354 for regular gasoline - a spread of about $1.85 per gallon. Diesel reached a nominal record of $6.29 per gallon in September, according to EIA, and remained above $6 nationally in early October.

That gap is not primarily the result of a sudden increase in diesel taxes or some new change in fuel specifications. Those structural factors help explain why diesel usually costs more than gasoline, but they do not explain why the premium is so large today. The current premium reflects a very tight global distillate market layered on top of the long-term changes that already made diesel the more expensive fuel.

That distinction is important because it separates the underlying reason diesel normally carries a premium from the temporary forces that can cause that premium to explode.

Refining Margins Are A Consequence, Not A Cause

Refining margins have risen sharply, and major refiners are benefiting from the tight market. But those high margins are a consequence of constrained diesel supply relative to demand rather than the original cause of the shortage.

When refinery capacity is disrupted, exports are curtailed, and inventories fall, the value of the remaining barrels rises. Refiners that can continue producing diesel benefit from that scarcity, but the scarcity comes first. This distinction is important because high margins are sometimes cited as evidence that refiners decided to raise prices, when in reality the margin expansion is largely the market's response to a shortage of refined product.

Diesel Is A Different Market Than Gasoline

The broader lesson is that gasoline and diesel may come from the same barrel of crude oil, but they are not interchangeable products. They serve different markets, have different seasonal demand patterns, require different processing, and face different global supply pressures. A refinery cannot simply turn every barrel of crude into whichever product happens to be most expensive that day because refinery configuration, crude quality, product specifications, and physical operating limits all constrain what can be produced.

That is why abundant crude oil does not guarantee cheap diesel. The United States can produce record amounts of oil, run refineries near capacity, and still face expensive diesel if global product markets remain tight.

Twenty years ago, gasoline was often the more expensive fuel. Then diesel moved to a structural premium, and today that premium has widened dramatically because the global market for diesel and other middle distillates is again under severe strain. Until those supply constraints ease, diesel is likely to remain much more expensive than gasoline.

title: "De-Risk As Fast As Possible": EU Eyes Vietnam For Critical Materials To Cut Alarming China Dependence
desc:
"De-Risk As Fast As Possible": EU Eyes Vietnam For Critical Materials To Cut Alarming China Dependence

Brussels appears increasingly aligned with the Trump administration's view that securing reliable, conflict-free supplies of critical materials is important for the incoming rearmament supercycle. Continued reliance on China exposes Western defense manufacturers to export restrictions that have already disrupted supply chains and could delay deliveries.

Reuters cites internal EU documents dated June 2026 that identified Vietnam as a potential source of critical materials outside China.

"Considering Europe's need to rearm and de-risk as fast as possible, the EU cannot afford ignoring Vietnam as a potential supplier of critical raw materials considering its abundant reserves in rare earth and tungsten in particular," the document stated which was prepared by the EU delegation in Hanoi.

The push comes as Chinese export restrictions collide with the West's rearmament supercycle next year, exposing alarming vulnerabilities in the supply chains needed to manufacture missiles, ammunition, armored vehicles, one-way attack drones, interceptors, sensors, and other military equipment.

The West is quickly learning that bigger and bigger defense budgets alone cannot solve the critical material shortage and there is high urgency in securing alternative supply chains.

Vietnam holds substantial deposits of tungsten, rare earths, and other critical minerals, but its exports to Europe have largely been limited to tungsten and antimony, both of which are used to manufacture weapons.

The document noted that China's restrictions on critical material exports last year disrupted European supply chains, strengthening the case for exploring alternative sources.

It called for stronger relations with Vietnam to "add an alternative to China," especially after Beijing's export restrictions last year "disrupted European supply chains."

"The European Commission is currently assessing the potential for concrete cooperation with Vietnam in the critical raw materials sector," a spokesperson for the EU executive arm told the outlet.

Adrien Rabier, Bernstein's equity analyst covering European aerospace and defense, outlined to clients last month that Europe's rearmament supercycle will begin next year and extend through the end of the decade.

Our reporting has pointed out that the next phase of the critical materials trade will favor miners already producing and delivering these materials to Western markets.

This comes as resource nationalism intensifies across critical minerals, metals, energy, adding to uncertainty as the world heads into a potentially volatile winter.

The VanEck Rare Earth and Strategic Metals ETF (REMX), which tracks global companies that produce, refine, and recycle critical minerals, peaked in May and lost nearly half its value by early fall.

REMX's decline appears to be a retracement of the rally in 2025 and early 2026 that followed China's export restrictions. Once the space bottoms, traders will likely focus on miners that can reliably deliver conflict-free materials to the West. These materials are critical not only to the rearmament cycle but also to AI data centers, reindustrialization, electrification, and the broader modern economy.

desc:
John Healey has spoken to UK journalists at the IMF annual meeting in Bangkok, and said banks are a part of the “jewel” in the UK’s economic crown

Today’s better-than-forecast UK growth report is good news for chancellor John Healey as he hobnobs with other finance ministers at the IMF meeting in Bangkok.

But it may encourage the Bank of England to raise interest rates as soon as its next meeting in November….

“While August’s unexpected uptick all but confirms that the OBR will raise its growth forecast for this year from 1.1% to 1.4%, the Chancellor still faces a major Budget headache, as elevated borrowing costs eat into fiscal headroom and increase pressure for tax rises.

“These unexpectedly upbeat figures will further embolden hawkish sentiment among policymakers by reinforcing the view that the economy is strong enough to withstand a rate rise, making a November hike look highly likely.”

“The latest GDP figures are encouraging, with the economy growing by 0.7% in the three months to August, its strongest growth rate since May. On its current trajectory, the UK is likely to record growth comfortably above 1% this year, which would probably be enough to make it the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7.

“The UK’s growth performance has been a bright spot amid a less impressive run of economic news following events in the Middle East. Business investment has been an important driver, particularly spending on ICT hardware, likely linked to the build-out of AI infrastructure. The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers.
